key_points: Growth signals are mixed. The Fed and its staff describe solid expansion driven by AI capex, initial claims are low at 215k, and equities are at record highs. Against that, the GDPNow reading is only ~1.3% (vs 2.9% a year ago), payroll gains were just +57k in June, and Michigan sentiment is very depressed at 49.5, though it is rebounding.

2y and 10y yields sit near the top of their 1-year ranges, which prices strength. A modest real-activity disappointment is the slightly more likely surprise, so yields lean mildly lower over 1-3 months, with the front end most sensitive.
Softer growth relative to hawkish pricing implies a slight bull-steepening tilt in 2s10s from a curve that is already flat (5th percentile).

Resilient AI investment and earnings momentum keep the growth read mildly supportive for the S&P 500. With HY spreads near cycle tights (2.69), there is limited room for further tightening, so the 3-month spread and VIX views are near neutral.

Staff see downside risks to growth. Slower global growth (Europe, lower-income Asia) gives a slight negative tilt to oil demand and a small negative tilt to the dollar via the rate-differential channel. Gold and breakevens get essentially no signal from this factor.
Inflation is high: CPI ~4.2% y/y through May, core PCE ~3.4% y/y; staff estimated May headline PCE 4.1%, core 3.4%.

Core expected to change little through year-end; price pressures described as broadening (non-housing services, AI-driven tech/electricity demand, tariff pass-through); staff and participants see upside risks.

Fed dropped easing bias, 'will deliver price stability'; many participants see appropriate rate above current range by year-end — sticky core data feeds hike pricing, mildly bullish front-end yields and the dollar, flattening 2s10s.

Offsetting: WTI fell ~23% in the past month, so upcoming June/July headline CPI should get energy relief; that weighs on headline and near-term breakevens, already at 10th percentile (2.24%), limiting downside.
Higher real-rate pressure from sticky core is a mild headwind for equities, gold and credit spreads, and a mild support for VIX; effects kept small since much is already priced.
Labor market stable-to-firm: unemployment fell to 4.2% in June, initial claims 215k and well below a year ago; payrolls +57k is modest but consistent with slow labor-force growth.

FOMC minutes say downside employment risks have moderated and labor is not a source of inflation; a firm labor market removes the case for cuts and keeps hike scenarios alive, a mild hawkish tilt for front-end yields.
Much is already priced: 2y at 99th percentile of its 1y range, so the labor signal only nudges yields up and the curve slightly flatter.
Stable employment supports earnings/credit: mild tightening bias for HY spreads, slight downward lean for VIX, slight support for dollar; gold slightly negative via firmer real rates.
Signal is weak: low claims leave asymmetric risk of softening, and upcoming jobs reports (early Aug, early Sep) could cut either way, so probabilities stay close to 0.50.

Fed funds sits at 3.50-3.75% (IORB 3.65%), but the 2y is at 4.21%, near its 1y high. Markets are pricing a hiking path, including a hike by mid-2027, while the Desk survey median shows no change into 2027 and then a cut.

The June minutes were hawkish: the easing bias was dropped, the statement now says 'will deliver price stability', a few participants saw a case for hikes, and many saw the appropriate year-end rate above the current range. The market has largely absorbed this; the 2y rose 7bp this week.

Since the meeting, WTI has fallen about 23% after the US-Iran MOU and breakevens have dropped. That erodes the energy-shock rationale for firming, so the July 29 and September 16 FOMC meetings are more likely to deliver holds than to validate the hike pricing.

Net, the policy factor tilts modestly toward lower front-end yields over 1-3 months, with the 2y falling more than the 10y. That points to a slightly steeper 2s10s from its 5th-percentile level and a mildly softer dollar as rate differentials narrow, with the ECB also hiking.
Second-order effects: less hike pricing modestly supports equities and gold, and slightly tightens HY spreads. VIX is near its lows, so FOMC event risk keeps that tilt small.
The near-term (1w) signal is weak because the hawkish minutes momentum persists until the July FOMC.
The early-August quarterly refunding falls inside the 1m window. With large deficits and coupon sizes high, the duration supply risk tilts 10y yields modestly higher via the term premium.

The NY Fed manager flagged a shift in Treasury ownership from price-insensitive official holders to price-sensitive private investors. That argues for a structurally firmer term premium and a steeper curve.
2s10s sits near the 5th percentile of its 1y range after front-end-led flattening. Supply and term premium pressure should mainly lift the long end, giving a mild steepening bias, especially at 3m.
Reserve management bill purchases and low bill supply anchor the front end. Fiscal factors give little signal for 2y yields, which are dominated by Fed expectations.
Fiscal concerns give a small headwind to the dollar and equities and a small tailwind to gold over longer horizons. Higher real long yields modestly pressure valuations and spreads at the 3m horizon.
Mid-September tax receipts and a TGA rebuild could drain reserves modestly. Effects on VIX and credit spreads are small; no debt-ceiling constraint is evident.

Financial conditions are very loose: NFCI -0.52, HY OAS 2.69 near 1y tights (5th pct), VIX 15 (10th pct); this supports risk assets near term but leaves asymmetric room for spread widening and vol mean reversion over 1-3 months.

Fed balance sheet is growing via reserve management bill purchases; reserves ample, repo traded 15bp below IORB in May and ON RRP take-up reappeared—money-market liquidity is abundant, slightly anchoring front-end/bill yields.

Desk flagged shift of Treasury ownership from price-insensitive official holders to price-sensitive private investors, a structural upward pressure on term premium—mild upside for 10y and 2s10s steepening.

Emerging stress in private credit (slowing BDC inflows, accelerating redemptions) and lower-income households leaning on credit are early cracks that argue against spreads staying at tights for 3 months.
Dollar long positioning in DX futures at 99th percentile with ample dollar liquidity tilts mildly toward dollar softness; gold mildly helped by balance-sheet expansion.
Dollar index futures net long sits at the 99th 52-week percentile (+24.9% of OI). This is a crowded long and the clearest contrarian signal: it leans toward dollar downside, more so over 1-3 months.

Risk complacency is high: S&P 500 at the 98th percentile of its 1y range, VIX 15 (10th percentile), HY OAS 2.69 (5th percentile). E-mini spec positioning is at the 93rd percentile, so it is relatively long. Together these mildly favor VIX and spread mean reversion higher, while momentum offsets the equity downside.

The 10y T-note spec short is mid-range (51st percentile), so no Treasury signal. The 2y net short is less extreme than usual (80th percentile) and was covered further, with the 2y yield at the 99th percentile of its range. That gives a slight lean to front-end yields easing and mild steepening.
WTI spec length is light (30th percentile) and was cut sharply (-34.8k) after a 23% monthly drop. Washed-out positioning gives a mild contrarian bounce bias.
Gold positioning is neutral (45th percentile) after a 15% 3m fall to the bottom of its range. Only a slight rebound tilt.
Breakevens at the 10th percentile of their range give a small mean-reversion-up lean.
The ECB has already hiked, and markets still price at least one more hike in both the euro area and the UK. That keeps foreign short rates rising.

The US-AFE 2-year gap widened over the last intermeeting period, but the increase since the Middle East conflict began is now similar across economies. Room for further US-favourable divergence looks limited.

Speculative long positioning in DX futures is at the 99th percentile of its 52-week range. That crowding leaves the dollar vulnerable to an unwind if foreign central banks keep tightening, so I give a modest downside bias to the broad dollar.

Rising foreign sovereign yields and the shift in Treasury ownership toward price-sensitive private holders point to global term-premium spillover. That tilts the 10-year up and the 2s10s curve steeper; the US 2-year is driven mostly by the Fed.

Growth abroad is weak in the euro area, Canada and Mexico, and the energy shock is hitting Europe and lower-income Asia. This is a mild drag on oil demand, offset by strong high-tech exports from Asia tied to the AI buildout.
A softer dollar and gold sitting near the bottom of its 1-year range give gold a slight upside bias. Effects on equities, HY spreads, breakevens and VIX are roughly neutral from this factor.

WTI at $72 is down 23% in a month after the US-Iran MOU and prospective Hormuz reopening; normalizing flows and inventory rebuild point to further drift lower, while a residual war premium in a likely backwardated curve adds to the downside bias. The risk of a deal breakdown keeps this bias modest.
Speculative crude length was cut sharply (CL net long down ~35k contracts, 30th percentile), so positioning is not a squeeze source. Last week's +3.9% bounce argues for a near-neutral 1-week call.

Fading energy pass-through should ease headline inflation over 2H as gasoline falls, a path the staff forecast already assumes. That leans breakevens lower even from the 10th percentile, with mild downward pressure on front-end yields via a less hawkish Fed path, so 2s10s modestly steeper.
Lower oil is a mild tailwind for equities and lower vol. HY spreads are near-neutral: easier inflation is offset by energy-sector credit drag.
The oil-shock dollar bid (terms of trade, rate differentials) unwinds slightly. Gold gets little support from commodity-inflation hedging demand.

The US-Iran memorandum of understanding and the prospective reopening of the Strait of Hormuz are now largely priced. WTI is down about 23% in a month, VIX is at 15, HY spreads sit at the 5th percentile and gold is at the 3rd percentile of its 1-year range.

With the peace largely priced in, the geopolitical tail is asymmetric. A breakdown or implementation hiccup would hit risk assets hard (VIX up, spreads wider, equities down, gold bid, oil spikes). Further normalization adds only modest additional relief.

For oil the two forces roughly offset. Continued Hormuz flow normalization could push WTI toward its pre-conflict levels (1-year low near $55), while deal-fragility risk premia could return. The last week's +3.9% bounce hints that some premium persists. Net near neutral, with slight downside at 3m as supply returns.

For yields the effect is ambiguous: an oil flare lifts breakevens and front-end hike pricing, while risk-off flight to quality pulls long yields down. I keep rates near 0.50 with only a slight bull tilt and a mild steepener on a risk-off scenario.
Gold has given back its war premium (-15% in 3m). Re-hedging demand after a fragile ceasefire gives a mild upward tilt.
Tariff pass-through is ongoing and the November midterms fall beyond the 3m window. Campaign-season trade and fiscal rhetoric adds mild headline-volatility risk but no strong directional signal.
The dollar gets slight support from safe-haven demand in shock scenarios; speculative dollar longs are already at the 99th percentile, which limits that effect.

thesis: The Fed has turned hawkish: the June minutes dropped the easing bias and flagged hike scenarios. The 2y sits at the 99th percentile of its range and already prices that path. Meanwhile WTI has fallen 23% since the US-Iran MOU, which undercuts the energy rationale for firming. July and September holds are therefore more likely than validation of the hikes, so I lean to lower front-end yields over 1-3 months. Term-premium pressure from the August refunding, price-sensitive Treasury ownership and global spillover keeps the 10y roughly flat. Together that gives a steepening bias in 2s10s from its 5th-percentile level. The dollar's speculative long is at the 99th percentile and foreign central banks are hiking, so I tilt the dollar lower. Gold sits near the bottom of its range and gets a mild rebound tilt. Financial conditions are very loose (VIX at the 10th percentile, HY OAS at the 5th) and the geopolitical tail is asymmetric, so spreads and VIX lean toward mean reversion higher at 1-3 months. Equity momentum and AI earnings keep the S&P biased up, near its base rate. Oil drifts modestly lower as Hormuz flows normalize, and breakevens are near neutral given their low level. The pooled log-odds overstate confidence because the views are correlated, so all probabilities are shrunk toward base rates.
